chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
title: How the Cavalcade show was staged and paid
summary: He wrote openers and closers for each star act; Teagarden got $1,000 a week and the printed magazine sold well at a dollar fifty.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Well, what did the show do? Did you sort of have a history of jazz, or what?

Yeah, we was playing concerts. Like, Jack Teagarden would play his trombone and he would do three or four numbers and sing. But I had it fixed so when he played, when he come out, I would have the reed section, because we had George ________ was on that show and Morris Loudon and Charlie Van Tour. I had the reed section open with him, just the opening number, one number. Then they'd disappear and he'd have it with the rhythm section.
And when he closed his act, I had the whole band to
close it and -- because he was at the bottom of the show. That that went on with all acts.
Was it a good band?
Oh, yeah. We didn't see any musicians on there. Everybody was a bandleader.
I see.

The top musicians. The way I wrote the opening, boy, everybody had a different manager. The manager wouldn't come to rehearsal. He say, I'm not going to come. Lips Page was on that show, too, you know?

But I wrote it so it stopped the squabble, because everybody was saying, who's going to start here, who's going to start here, and I handled all of that. I made an opening for Ed, a whole show. A whole show opening, except singers.
So it was like a concert presentation.

A whole show opener. The closer came, I think Red Ryder would be the first. So you introduce him and when he got ready to play his number Jesse Hickenbotham and -- no, yeah, Jesse Hickenbotham and Georgie and another horn, the reed section, would come out and just step right up on the stage and play background so they'd have at least three horns.
And then they'd leave and he'd take it over, talking and doing his little things. And when he closed his last number, the same three horns would come back (inaudible).
That must have been pretty good then.
(Inaudible) Dinah sang. George Jenkins was in the show and he did a special. I opened the second half with just the rhythm section one time.
Was it successful?

Yep. We was paying Jack Teagarden $1,000 a week, rain or shine. I was getting $500, Hickenbotham $500, -- no Hick was getting $350, George was getting $500, and you know what's happened? They were getting eight and ten dollars at the door back then, everywhere. We went all out in Nebraska and everywhere. Jack Teagarden was a big man, and sometimes he didn't work for three days a week. He still made all kinds of money. And we sold a lot of magazines, too, because they printed up the whole show in that, and had it just as the -- I'll show it to you -- just as the opening of the program, and the name, and it tells you, Eddie Durham wrote the show and all this, just as we was (inaudible). And sold $150 worth of magazines during the first intermission. Stack them up there, and the guy selling them a dollar and a half a magazine.
That's pretty far back to be getting that kind of money, but that was big people at that time, Dinah and Hickenbotham.
Did you play guitar in this at all?
Yeah, played guitar the second opening

show (unintelligible). Because that's where we wrote the second half. And that was -- and I got a writeup (unintelligible) in the paper, they had my picture, about that big. They didn't like (unintelligible). Because they did get drunk, boy.
I'll show you that magazine, maybe you can make a copy of it.
